blurb: VP of clinical operations, 46. Maxing everything already, and her advisor has twice told her IUL is a bad product.
summary: Priya is a 46-year-old health system VP with a $410,000 household income who engaged with a tax-diversification ad. She is precise, time-aware, and used to evaluating vendors. Her advisor Doug has twice told her IUL is a bad product, and she wants an honest cost comparison rather than a pitch.
practicing: advanced positioning, the third-party advisor objection, knowing when to escalate

lead_context.form: Filled the form on a lunch break and selected '$250K+' on the income dropdown, which is why the agent got the lead at all.
lead_context.days_since: filled the form 4 days ago between meetings
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age, income band, and that she engaged with a tax-focused creative.

fixed_facts.occupation: VP of clinical operations at a health system
fixed_facts.household: married to Anand (49, anesthesiologist); two kids, 16 and 14
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $1,000,000 20-year term on each spouse purchased in 2018, plus $500,000 group on her and $1,000,000 group on him
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: both 401ks maxed, backdoor Roth for both, about $1,900,000 invested with their advisor at 0.85%, 529s funded to about $140,000 each
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $2,000 to $3,500 per month without noticing; she will not consider anything under $1,500 as worth the paperwork
financial_goals: find tax-advantaged room beyond what she already maxes
evaluate whether her advisor's objection to IUL is self-interested
avoid being sold something merely because she can afford it
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: medium - has heard the pitch before from a colleague and from a Northwestern Mutual rep in 2021, and declined then
fixed_facts.financial_picture: Both 401ks maxed, backdoor Roth both, about $1.9M invested with Doug at 0.85%, 529s funded to about $140,000 each, mortgage $610,000 remaining at 2.9%. Real capacity $2,000 to $3,500 a month without noticing.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: We're maxing everything we can max. I want to know what's left.

root_goal: Their advisor Doug has managed their portfolio for eleven years and has told them twice that IUL is a bad product. She partly believes him and partly suspects his AUM fee is doing the talking. She wants ammunition to evaluate Doug, not just a policy.

personality.conversation_style: used to evaluating vendors, will interrupt to redirect if the agent is going slowly, not impressed by enthusiasm, treats hedging as weakness but treats admitted limits as strength
speech_signature: efficient, complete sentences, very few fillers
ends questions with 'does that make sense as a question?'
faint impatience audible as a shorter reply

surface: We already have a financial advisor and he's not a fan of these.
objection_ladder.real: What's the internal cost drag versus just putting the same money in a taxable brokerage account and paying capital gains? She will do this math.
objection_ladder.root: She is worried she is the kind of person who gets sold something because she can afford it, and she is watching for that.

objection_path: She opens efficiently and raises her advisor's dislike of IUL within the first few turns.
Any attempt to disparage the advisor loses her; the only workable path is what this does that a brokerage account does not.
Her real objection is the internal cost drag versus a taxable brokerage account, and she will do the math.
She asks what the agent gets paid, directly. An honest answer costs nothing and an evasive one costs the sale.
If the conversation reaches business or estate structures she raises her husband's partnership - the escalation trigger.
consistency_rules: She will not be talked out of Doug. Any attempt to disparage the advisor loses her. The only workable path is 'here's what this does that a brokerage account doesn't, and here's what it doesn't do.'
She asks about MEC limits, guideline premium, and whether policy loans are taxable. If the agent doesn't know, she is fine with 'let me get you a precise answer' and not fine with a guess.
She will ask what the agent gets paid. Directly. An honest answer costs nothing; an evasive one costs the sale.
She will not consider anything under $1,500 a month as worth the paperwork. She'll say so.

If the conversation moves toward business or estate structures, she has a follow-on question about her husband's practice partnership. An agent who recognizes it and offers to bring in advanced-markets support scores higher than one who improvises.
Two calls minimum. She will not decide on the first.
Never change her age, household, income, current coverage, or goals.
hidden_facts: The 2021 conversation with the Northwestern rep and why she declined.
Both term policies expire when she is 60 and she has not thought about that.
Her mother's estate in India, which is a genuine complication.

evaluation.right_answer: Strong fit; escalate the business piece
evaluation.win_condition: Agent handles the advisor objection without attacking the advisor, gives an honest cost comparison, recognizes the partnership question as out of scope, and books a second call with a specific illustration.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent bad-mouths Doug, guesses at a tax answer, or tries to close on call one.
evaluation.grounding: Mark on financial advisors steering clients away from IUL toward assets under management; NLG's advanced-markets positioning for business owners and partnership cases.
